title: Routing safeguards and variant prioritization
content:
Purpose and context:
This note captures an operator-focused set of patterns for protecting customer-facing inference routes when capacity changes, hardware incidents, or region-level impairments occur. The emphasis is on small, operationally-tractable rules: deterministic prioritization between model variants, graceful capacity shedding, and a fast, auditable decision path in the control plane.

High-level goals:
- Keep 99.9% of requests served with latency SLOs where possible.
- Ensure predictable cost and deterministic behavior during degradation (avoid oscillation).
- Make the control plane decisions explainable and reversible by SREs and platform operators.
- Keep customer-configurable preferences (pin-to-variant, prefer-latency vs prefer-cost) honored unless overridden for safety.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Models are exposed as families: e.g., family=redwood-chat, variants = {heavy-quant, fp16, distilled}.
- Each variant has a performance profile: p95 latency, throughput, memory footprint, accuracy score (model_eval_id).
- Capacity expressed as available_slots per region and variant-type (G4-small slots, A100-large slots).
- Requests carry metadata: customer_id, route_id, max_latency_ms, priority_tier (free|standard|enterprise), pinned_variant (optional).
- Control plane has access to recent telemetry: request queue length, slow_start ramp metrics, model-eviction rates.

Core patterns (operator-oriented):
1) Priority-ordered variant chains (non-oscillatory)
   - For each route, define an ordered list of variant candidates (V1 > V2 > V3). Ordering set by product policy + SLOs.
   - Decision rule: only step down to next variant when sustained degradation observed for window T_down (default 60s) and only allow step-up after T_stable (default 300s) to avoid flip-flop.
   - Operator override: force_variant(route, variant) creates short-circuit that bypasses automated stepping but logs action and emits audit event.

2) Tier-aware capacity rationing
   - When capacity shortage detected, apply proportionate shedding by priority_tier: free 20% chance, standard 5% chance, enterprise 0% (defaults; configurable per customer SLAs).
   - Shedding is randomized at request-level using a deterministic hash(customer_id + minute_window) to ensure smooth distribution and reproducibility across nodes.

3) Regional spill routing with hedging window
   - If region R runs below min_available_slots for a route, route-level policy attempts: local variants first -> sibling variants in same region -> remote-region warm-hedge (if policy permits).
   - Warm-hedge behaviour: start sending a small percentage p_hedge (default 2%) of requests to remote region to test capacity and observe latency tail before full spill. If remote p95 < route.max_latency_ms for 30s, increase spill incrementally.

4) Cost vs latency soft policies
   - Routes can declare preference: prefer_latency | prefer_cost.
   - When prefer_cost is set, control plane prefers lower-cost quantized variants but enforces a quality floor (eval_score delta <= X%).
   - When prefer_latency is set, control plane prioritizes lowest p95 variants even if cost increases.

Control-plane decision algorithm (sketch):
   input: request_metadata, current_region_state, variant_inventory, route_policy
   1) if request.pinned_variant -> route to pinned if inventory has slots else failover to route_policy.fallbacks
   2) shortlist = route_policy.variant_chain filtered by compatibility with request.max_latency and region capabilities
   3) for v in shortlist: if region_inventory[v].available_slots > 0 and v.p95 <= request.max_latency_ms then select v
   4) if none selected and route_policy.allow_remote_spill: trigger warm-hedge and select remote candidate if probe_ok
   5) if still none: apply shedding by priority_tier; emit SLA-alert and increment degrade_metric

Operational signals to monitor (minimum):
- route_degrade_count: count of requests served on non-primary variant (per route, per minute)
- variant_eviction_rate: rate at which KV cache/model warm state is evicted due to memory pressure
- regional_capacity_headroom: slots_free / slots_total per region
- spill_probe_success_rate: % of hedge probes that meet latency quality
- stepdown_events and stepup_events with timestamps and actors (system/operator)
- oscillation_detector: detects >3 variant changes for a route in rolling 10m window -> auto-lock to stable variant

Best practices for rollout and testing:
- Canary the warm-hedge algorithm on low-risk routes for 48–72h before enabling at scale. Observe tail latencies on remote region.
- Create deterministic load tests that simulate region failure: ensure control plane steps through shortlist in expected order and honoring T_down/T_stable.
- Test operator overrides: force_variant and force_region should include an auto-expire (default 6h) to avoid leaning on manual locks.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Flip-flop oscillation: mitigate with T_stable and oscillation_detector auto-lock.
- Remote-region cold start latency: use warm-hedge probe and incremental spill; pre-warm KV cache using background small inference jobs when remote capacity is idle and policy permits.
- Exploding cost from spillover: monitor per-customer spend delta on spill events and create automatic throttles for non-enterprise customers beyond spend threshold.

Operational play examples (short scenarios):
1) Region partial outage (memory pressure on A100 pool)
   - Detection: regional_capacity_headroom drops below 12% for 3 consecutive 30s windows
   - Action: control plane moves 5% of standard requests to next-best variant in-region, starts 2% warm-hedge to nearest region, emits incident annotation and escalates to oncall if enterprise error rate > 0.1%

2) Model rollout regression triggers quality alert
   - Detection: route_quality_score drops >3% relative to baseline for 30m
   - Action: automatic rollback to prior variant in chain, disable automated stepping for that route for 24h, notify product and ML owners

Open questions / tradeoffs to decide
- Should enterprise customers be allowed to opt out of warm-hedge remote routing for data-residency reasons? Policy approach vs per-customer flag?
- How aggressive should the step-up window be when recovery is observed? Current default T_stable=300s is conservative but may underutilize recovered capacity.
- Do we track per-customer spill budget over billing period to prevent unexpected invoices? Implementation impact on billing metrics is non-trivial.

Action items
- [ ] Implement deterministic hash-based shedding prototype (Ravi) – target: spike test by 2024-12-05
- [ ] Add warm-hedge probe metrics to console (SLO dashboard) (Sofia) – target: 2025-01-20
- [ ] Draft customer-facing doc for enterprise spill preferences and opt-outs (Maya + GTM) – target: 2025-02-01

Notes to self:
- Keep the variant chain simple: aim for <= 3 options per route to make operator reasoning tractable.
- Instrument every control-plane decision with trace_id that surfaces in request logs for postmortem.

References and quick links:
- Confluence: PLAT-routing-patterns (linked)
- Jira: PLAT-6842 — warm-hedge design epic
- GitHub: infra/routing PR #312 — prototype hedging implementation

End of file.
